title: Isolation on a real OS, then the MCU contrast
objective: Boot xv6 under QEMU from the official MIT 6.1810 materials, show a user process and one syscall or trap, and write a four-row UNIX-versus-MCU contrast a mentor can check.
whyThisMatters: An edge node often has no process boundary. If you cannot name what xv6 buys with virtual memory and syscalls, you will over-trust firmware that shares one address space with every driver.
evidence: A captured xv6-under-QEMU session (or official 6.1810 lab output) showing a user process and a syscall or trap
A source citation (file and function name) for the trap or syscall path you exercised
MCU-CONTRAST.md with four named rows — isolation unit, memory protection, privileged transition, failure mode — each with a UNIX/xv6 column and an MCU/RTOS column
A paragraph in MCU-CONTRAST.md stating one security property xv6 gets from virtual memory that a Cortex-M0 without an MPU does not
Reflection notes answering the task questions
acceptanceCriteria: The captured session log shows xv6 (or the official 6.1810 user environment) running under QEMU and includes a user-level command or program plus evidence of a syscall or trap (kernel print, strace-equivalent, or a breakpoint note with the trap function name).
MCU-CONTRAST.md has four rows titled isolation unit, memory protection, privileged transition, and failure mode; each row has a UNIX/xv6 mechanism and a corresponding MCU or RTOS mechanism.
MCU-CONTRAST.md contains a paragraph that names one security property provided by xv6 virtual memory and states that a Cortex-M0-class core without an MPU does not have that property.
The source citation names a file and function from the 6.1810/xv6 tree (for example trampoline/usertrap or syscall), not a blog paraphrase.
